title: HIV Prevention Funding Cuts Leave Immigrant Communities Without a Safety Net
excerpt: Federal grant terminations and proposed budget cuts totaling $1.5 billion threaten decades of progress against HIV, with Latino and immigrant populations bearing the heaviest burden as ICE enforcement drives patients away from clinics.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Proposed $1.5 billion cut to HIV programs threatens decades of progress in prevention.
  • CDC provides over 90% of federal HIV prevention funding, facing significant budget cuts.
  • Eliminating funding could lead to 143,000 new infections and 127,000 AIDS-related deaths in five years.
  • ICE enforcement has drastically reduced HIV testing among Latino populations, with some clinics seeing 50% fewer clients.
  • The Trump administration's FY2026 budget proposes a $1.5 billion (35%) cut to domestic HIV programs, including the elimination of all CDC prevention funding and the Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative.
  • The CDC provides more than 90% of federal HIV prevention funding — about $1 billion annually — and has already eliminated half its HIV branch offices.
  • Cutting federal prevention funds could lead to 143,000 additional HIV infections and 127,000 AIDS-related deaths within five years, according to the Foundation for AIDS Research.
  • ICE enforcement operations have caused HIV testing among Latino populations to drop dramatically, with some clinics reporting a 50% decrease in new clients.

A Billion-Dollar Safety Net Unravels

When Eldridge Dwayne Ellis drives the My Brother's Keeper mobile testing clinic through Jackson, Mississippi, people come not just for HIV tests but for a rare point of contact with the healthcare system. "People see us as their only outlet, not just for testing but for confidential conversations, for a shoulder to cry on," Ellis told KFF Health News. "I don't understand how someone, with the stroke of a pen, could just haphazardly write off the health of millions."

That pen has been busy. The Trump administration's May 2 budget proposal for fiscal 2026 targets $3.59 billion in CDC cuts, and its drafted plan for the Department of Health and Human Services eliminates all prevention funding at the agency. In April, the CDC shuttered half of its 10 HIV branch offices, laying off staff who had overseen the rollout of grants to health departments and community organizations.

The CDC provides more than 90% of all federal HIV prevention funding — roughly $1 billion a year. The administration's FY2026 request represents a $1.5 billion decline, or 35%, compared to FY2025 levels, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation. It would also eliminate the Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative, a program Trump himself launched during his first term.

The Human Cost in Numbers

The Foundation for AIDS Research, or amfAR, estimates that eliminating federal HIV prevention funding would result in more than 143,000 additional infections and about 127,000 additional AIDS-related deaths in the United States within five years. Excess medical costs would exceed $60 billion.

Community organizations across the South have already scaled back. My Brother's Keeper lost a $12 million NIH grant, a CDC health-disparities award, and laboratory funding for detecting HIV and sexually transmitted infections. Mississippi's AIDS Services Coalition froze its HIV testing clinic and paused mobile outreach at homeless shelters, colleges, and churches. Five Southern states — Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Mississippi, and Missouri — contributed zero state funds to HIV prevention last year, making them entirely dependent on federal grants.

"When you are in the South, you need the federal government. When we had slavery, we needed the federal government. When we had the push for civil rights, we needed the federal government. And we still need the federal government for health care."

— June Gipson, CEO, My Brother's Keeper

Immigrant Communities Face a Double Threat

For immigrant communities, the funding cuts compound an already dire situation. Latino populations are 72% more likely than the general U.S. population to be diagnosed with HIV, and new infections among Latinos increased 24% between 2010 and 2022. Federal programs that funded bilingual outreach workers, culturally aligned health providers, and community testing sites are among those being eliminated.

Immigration enforcement has made access worse. In Minnesota, where ICE's Operation Metro Surge deployed over 3,000 agents beginning in December, HIV testing among Latino populations has "dropped dramatically," according to the state's health department commissioner. The Aliveness Project, a Minneapolis community wellness center specializing in HIV care, reported a more than 50% decrease in new clients.

Fear of deportation is pushing patients off their medications. Clinicians at Aliveness Project have had to transition patients off injectable HIV treatments — which require in-clinic visits — back to oral medications that had previously proven less effective for them. Some providers are delivering medication to patients' homes and pausing routine lab work to limit in-person visits.

"Some of these patients will die in their home country," said Anna Person, chair of the HIV Medicine Association. "It's a death sentence."

Diaspora Health Access Under Pressure

The crisis extends beyond Latino communities to South Asian and other immigrant populations who rely on federally funded community health centers for HIV testing and preventive services like PrEP, the pre-exposure prophylaxis drug that can cost over $28,000 a year without assistance programs. With 644,000 people in the United States currently on PrEP, the proposed cuts to Medicaid and the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies are dramatically increasing the number of uninsured individuals — a burden that falls disproportionately on immigrant families navigating complex healthcare systems.

Advocacy groups have averted $3.5 billion in proposed HIV funding cuts so far, and a federal judge has temporarily blocked $600 million in grant terminations targeting four Democrat-led states. But public health experts warn that the sustained uncertainty is itself causing harm.

"We have all the tools, and yet we are staring down this rollback of infrastructure and research dollars, prevention efforts, treatment efforts, that are going to put us squarely back in the 1980s," said Person. "There seems to be no other rationale for that besides cruelty."
